content.title: About
content.content: White beans (NFS) are dried beans from the Phaseolus vulgaris species. They have a light cream color, a mild nutty flavor, and a soft, creamy texture when cooked. The beans are commonly used in soups, stews, salads, and as a side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: White beans belong to the legume family and are among the oldest cultivated crops.
The NFS (Non‑Fatty Seed) variety is noted for its low fat content compared to other beans.
Beans are rich in complex carbohydrates that release energy slowly, helping maintain stable blood sugar levels.
Traditional cuisines worldwide feature white beans in dishes such as French cassoulet and Italian pasta e fagioli.
Dry beans can be stored for up to a year in a cool, dry place.

items.title: High in plant protein
items.content: A 100 g serving provides about 21 g of protein, making it an excellent source for vegetarians and vegans.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestive health, promotes satiety, and helps regulate cholesterol levels.

items.title: Source of iron and folate
items.content: Iron is essential for oxygen transport, while folate is important for DNA synthesis and anemia prevention.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The NFS variety contains less than 1 % fat, suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Potassium and magnesium in the beans help maintain healthy blood pressure.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Beans contain phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption; soaking and cooking reduce its effect.

items.title: Raw toxicity
items.content: Raw beans contain lectins that can be harmful; they must be fully cooked.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: Gas production
items.content: Beans can cause increased gas in sensitive people; gradual introduction to the diet can lessen this effect.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Before cooking, soak the beans in water for at least 8 hours, then drain and boil for 60–90 minutes until tender. Cooked beans can be added to soups, salads, stews, mashed into spreads, or used in vegetarian patties.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry beans in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Cooked beans should be cooled and kept in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days, or frozen for up to 3 months.
